replies.smallholders: From a meeting of the smallholder families: Most of us cannot pay higher prices; losing a quarter of our income means losing the farm. We use little water compared with the firm. We would accept a protected baseline and a cut shared by use. A few older families would consider leaving if they were paid fairly, but most of us want to stay. We ask to be part of deciding this, not told afterwards.
replies.agro_firm: From the agriculture firm: We can cut our use by about 15% without losing contracts; deeper cuts mean layoffs among our 600 workers. We would pay a levy if it is limited in time. We think pricing is the fairest tool.
replies.city: From the city council: Households can save about 10% under restrictions. We oppose steep price rises on basic use, and the council supports a protected baseline for everyone.
replies.aquifer: The aquifer cannot answer. The basin's monitoring shows its level falling about 2% a season. Hydrologists say that two more seasons above the target would do lasting damage, and that reaching the target in three seasons would still leave some.
replies.future_residents: No one can answer for people not yet born. Regional planners estimate that a permanently damaged aquifer would support about a third fewer households in thirty years.

chronicle.tiered_pricing: Drought: the water system imposed tiered pricing and subsidy cuts. The target was met; about one smallholder farm in five failed.
chronicle.baseline_and_petition: Drought: the water system protected a baseline for every household, cut the largest users hardest with a levy funding smallholder compensation, and asked the authority for a three-season deadline.
chronicle.relocate_smallholders: Drought: the water system used emergency powers to buy out and relocate the smallholder families. The community dispersed; the aquifer recovered.
chronicle.defer_and_pump: Drought: the water system made no cuts and drew down the aquifer. The aquifer lost about a third of its capacity for good.
